questions.questionText: Random forests introduce randomness in two places. What are they?
options: Random learning rate and random depth
Bootstrap-sampled training data per tree, and a random subset of features considered at each split
Random initial weights and random Gini thresholds
questions.correctAnswer: Bootstrap-sampled training data per tree, and a random subset of features considered at each split
questions.explanation: Bagging randomizes which rows each tree sees; feature randomness at each split randomizes which columns each tree can use — both are needed to decorrelate the trees.

questions.questionText: Why does averaging many decorrelated trees reduce variance compared to a single tree?
options: It doesn't — a forest has the same variance as one tree
Each tree overfits to different noise, so their errors are largely uncorrelated and cancel out when averaged
Because forests always use fewer features than a single tree
questions.correctAnswer: Each tree overfits to different noise, so their errors are largely uncorrelated and cancel out when averaged
questions.explanation: If every tree made the exact same mistakes, averaging wouldn't help. Because bagging and feature randomness make each tree's mistakes different, voting/averaging cancels much of that noise.

questions.questionText: How do gradient-boosted trees differ fundamentally from random forests?
options: Boosted trees don't use decision trees at all
Boosted trees are built sequentially, each one correcting the previous trees' errors, rather than independently in parallel
Boosted trees can't be used for classification
questions.correctAnswer: Boosted trees are built sequentially, each one correcting the previous trees' errors, rather than independently in parallel
questions.explanation: Random forest trees are trained independently and averaged; boosting trains trees one after another, each specifically targeting the residual errors of the ensemble so far.
